title: Traps, Rumors, and a Wall Finished in Fifty-Two Days
summary: With the wall nearly done, Nehemiah's enemies change tactics. They invite him four times to a meeting where they mean to harm him, send an open letter accusing him of planning a revolt, and hire a prophet to frighten him into hiding in the temple. Nehemiah sees through each scheme and keeps working, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days, leaving the surrounding nations afraid because they recognize God's hand in it.
story: The opposition that began with mockery in chapter 4 now aims directly at Nehemiah himself. If the workers could not be stopped, perhaps the leader could be removed, discredited, or frightened into a mistake. The chapter is the climax of the building account: verse 15 records the completion of the wall, the goal set in chapter 2. It also shows that the danger was not only outside. Some of Judah's own nobles were tied to Tobiah by marriage and oath, and a prophet within the community was willing to be hired against Nehemiah. The finished wall will be followed in chapter 7 by the task of filling the city with people, and in chapter 8 by the reading of the law.
historical:
The wall's completion on the twenty-fifth of Elul (verse 15) falls in late summer, probably around September 445 BC, since Nehemiah had arrived earlier in Artaxerxes' twentieth year. Fifty-two days is fast, but much of the old foundation could be reused, the work was divided among many teams (chapter 3), and the circuit Nehemiah rebuilt was smaller than the city of the late monarchy.

Geshem the Arab (verse 1) was a powerful figure in the Arabian region south of Judah. Many scholars connect him with the Geshem named as father of a king of Kedar on a silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt, which would make him a leader of the Kedarite Arabs, a significant power in the Persian period. The plain of Ono (verse 2) lay near the coast, near Lod, well northwest of Jerusalem, and on the border of Judah's territory: a meeting there would have taken Nehemiah far from his people and into a place his enemies could control. The charge of rebellion in verses 6-7 was dangerous because an earlier attempt to rebuild the walls had already been stopped by royal order on just such grounds (Ezra 4:12-22).
cultural:
Letters in the Persian period were normally rolled or folded and sealed, so that only the recipient read them. Sanballat's letter comes unsealed (verse 5), which means it was meant to be read by the messenger and anyone else along the way. It was a way of spreading the rumor while pretending merely to report it. The accusation that Nehemiah had appointed prophets to proclaim him king drew on real history: in Israel prophets had anointed kings, and Haggai and Zechariah had spoken hopefully about Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, a generation or two earlier.

Shemaiah's advice (verse 10) depended on the rules of the temple. The inner sanctuary was restricted to priests, and the law warned that an outsider who came near would be put to death (Numbers 18:7). King Uzziah had been struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). For Nehemiah, a layman, to hide inside the temple building would have been both a sin and a public act of cowardice, and either would have destroyed his authority. The mention of Noadiah the prophetess (verse 14) shows that there were several prophetic voices in Jerusalem at this time, some of whom opposed Nehemiah.
literary: The chapter is built from three schemes and three answers. The invitation to Ono (verses 2-4) is met with the refusal “I am doing a great work and cannot come down”. The open letter (verses 5-9) is met with a flat denial and a prayer for strength. The hired prophecy (verses 10-14) is met with the rhetorical questions of verse 11 and a prayer that God remember the plotters. Then comes the notice of completion (verse 15) and its effect on the nations (verse 16), after which a short postscript (verses 17-19) reveals the network of letters between Tobiah and the nobles of Judah. Nehemiah's brief prayers break into the narrative at verses 9 and 14, as they do throughout the memoir.

outline.t: Four invitations to the plain of Ono
An open letter accusing Nehemiah of rebellion
Shemaiah's false prophecy and the hired prophets
The wall is completed in fifty-two days
Tobiah's allies among the nobles of Judah

doctrines.note: When the wall is done, even the enemies recognize “that this task had been accomplished by our God” (verse 16). Human effort, planning, and courage filled the fifty-two days, yet the result is credited to God.

Nehemiah discerns that “God had not sent him” (verse 12). The chapter shows that a message spoken in God's name must be tested, especially when it urges disobedience to God's law or serves someone's interests.
Short, direct prayers punctuate Nehemiah's decisions: “But now, my God, strengthen my hands” (verse 9). Prayer here is not withdrawal from the conflict but strength for continuing in it.

words.note: Yare, to fear. The verb appears repeatedly (verses 9, 13, 14, 19), and in this chapter it is the enemies' main weapon: they try to make Nehemiah and the people afraid. Elsewhere in Nehemiah the same root describes the fear of God (5:9, 15). The chapter implies that one who fears God rightly is freed from being ruled by fear of people.

Raphah, to slacken or sink. The enemies say the builders' hands will drop from the work (verse 9). The phrase for weak or sinking hands is a common Hebrew picture of discouragement, and Nehemiah answers it with the opposite prayer, that God would strengthen his hands.

Nevuah, prophecy. Shemaiah's words have the form of prophecy, but Nehemiah recognizes that they were bought by his enemies (verse 12). The word reminds readers that the form of a divine message proves nothing; the source and the content must agree with what God has already said.

Shalem, to complete or finish. The wall is completed (verse 15). The root is related to shalom, peace or wholeness, and the completion of the wall marks the end of Jerusalem's long state of breach and disgrace.

christ: The link here is thematic. Nehemiah refuses to come down from the work God gave him, will not save his own life by stepping outside God's law, and is falsely accused of claiming to be king of the Jews. The Gospels tell of one who set his face toward Jerusalem and could not be turned aside, who would not save himself (Mark 15:30-31), and who was executed by an imperial governor under the written charge that he was King of the Jews. The comparison is not a prediction in Nehemiah, and Nehemiah does not suffer as Jesus did. But the pattern of faithful work pursued through slander and pressure is one the New Testament holds up for all who follow Christ (1 Corinthians 15:58).
questions: Nehemiah said, “I am doing a great work and cannot come down.” What distractions, even reasonable-sounding ones, pull you away from what you are called to do?
Shemaiah's advice sounded spiritual and protective, but it would have led Nehemiah into sin. How can a person tell good counsel from manipulation dressed in religious language?
Some of Judah's nobles kept praising Tobiah to Nehemiah because of their family ties. How do loyalties and relationships shape what we are willing to see about people?
